prompt: A function declares `var s string` and, without assigning it, prints it with `fmt.Printf("%#v\n", s)`. What appears?
hint: Every type has a zero value.

choices.why: Right. The zero value of a string is the empty string, and `%#v` writes it with its quotes.

choices.text: `<nil>`
choices.why: That is what an interface holding nothing prints. A string is not one of the kinds whose zero is `nil`.

choices.text: Whatever bytes were in that memory before
choices.why: That is C's rule for an unassigned local. Go sets every variable to its zero value when it is declared.

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler refuses to read `s` before it is assigned
choices.why: Some languages refuse that; Go does not need to, because `s` already holds a value from the moment it is declared.

prompt: Which of these types have `nil` as their zero value? Choose all that apply.
hint: Section 01 read the output in three groups.

choices.text: `*int`
choices.why: Yes: a pointer that points at nothing is `(*int)(nil)`.

choices.text: `[]int`
choices.why: Yes: `[]int(nil)`, and its length is 0.
An array is zero all the way down: `[3]int{0, 0, 0}`, never `nil`.

choices.text: `map[string]int`
choices.why: Yes: `map[string]int(nil)`, which can be read and not written.

choices.text: a struct type such as `point`
choices.why: A struct's zero is each field at its own zero: `main.point{X:0, Y:0, Label:""}`.

prompt: `var m map[string]int` and then `fmt.Println(len(m), m["a"])`. What happens?
hint: Reading and writing are not the same for a nil map.

choices.text: It panics, because `m` is nil
choices.why: Only writing to a nil map panics. Reading a key and asking its length both work.

choices.text: It prints `0 <nil>`
choices.why: A missing key gives the map's value type's zero, and that type is `int`, so it is `0`.

choices.text: It prints `0 0`
choices.why: Right. A nil map has length 0, and reading any key gives the zero `int`.

choices.text: It does not compile, because `m` was never made with `make`
choices.why: The compiler cannot know and does not ask. `make` matters only once you write to the map.

prompt: You write `type Counter struct { hits int; seen map[string]bool }`. Somebody declares `var c Counter` and your code runs `c.seen["/home"] = true`. What happens?
hint: What is the zero value of the field `seen`?

choices.text: It works: a field's zero map is an empty map ready for use
choices.why: That is true of `strings.Builder`, not of a map. A map field starts `nil`, and a nil map cannot be written.

choices.text: It panics, because `seen` is a nil map
choices.why: Right. This type's zero value is not ready to use. Lesson 14 shows the panic and the `make` that prevents it.

choices.text: It does not compile until `c` is initialised
choices.why: `var c Counter` already initialised it, to its zero value. The compiler accepts the write.

choices.text: The write is ignored and `seen` stays empty
choices.why: Go does not drop a write in silence. The write to a nil map stops the program with a panic.

prompt: `go doc strings.Builder` says, in its own words: "The zero value is ready to ___."
hint: Three letters: what you can do with it straight away.

prompt: Inside a `const` block, what is `iota`?
hint: Look at `Saturday`, on the seventh line of its block.

choices.text: A counter that goes up by one every time it is read
choices.why: It is fixed per line: two uses on the same line give the same number.

choices.text: The position of the line in its block, counting from 0
choices.why: Right. `Sunday` is on line 0 and `Saturday` on line 6, and a new block starts again at 0.

choices.text: The number of constants the package has declared so far
choices.why: It restarts in every block: the sizes block began at 0 again after the days.

choices.text: A keyword that turns the block into an enum type
choices.why: Go has no enum type and `iota` is not a keyword; `go doc builtin` lists it as a predeclared constant.

prompt: In the block `_ = iota`, `KiB = 1 << (10 * iota)`, `MiB`, `GiB`, `TiB`, how many bytes is `MiB`?
hint: `MiB` is on line 2 and repeats the expression above it.

prompt: Why does the program give line 0 of the `Status` block to `Unknown` instead of to `Active`?
hint: What does a field nobody set hold?

choices.text: Because `iota` cannot be used for a value of 0
choices.why: It can and was: `Sunday` is 0. The choice is about what 0 should mean.

choices.text: So a forgotten field says it was never set
choices.why: Right. The forgotten field holds the zero `Status`, and naming 0 `Unknown` makes it say so.

choices.text: Because Go requires the first constant of a block to be unused
choices.why: There is no such rule; the days block uses its first line for `Sunday`.

choices.text: Because 0 is reserved for errors in Go
choices.why: Errors are values of type `error`, not numbers; nothing reserves 0.

prompt: `fmt.Println(Monday)` with the lesson's own `Weekday` prints `1`, and `fmt.Println(time.Monday)` prints `Monday`. Why the difference?
hint: Both are declared with `iota` in the same way.

choices.text: `time`'s constants are strings, and ours are numbers
choices.why: `go doc time.Sunday` showed `Sunday Weekday = iota`, and `%d` printed `time.Saturday` as 6: they are numbers.

choices.text: `fmt` has a list of the standard library's names
choices.why: `fmt` knows nothing about `time`; it asks the value's type how to print itself.

choices.text: `time.Weekday` has a method that turns the number into a word
choices.why: Right. The constant is the number 1 in both; `time`'s type also has a `String` method, which lesson 25 covers.

choices.text: Our constants lost their names because of `iota`
choices.why: A constant's name never reaches the running program, with `iota` or without it.

prompt: A program saved `Weekday` numbers to a database last week. Today you insert a line `Holiday` between `Monday` and `Tuesday` in the `iota` block. What happens to the saved rows?
hint: Count the lines again after the insert.

choices.text: Every saved day from 2 upwards now reads as the wrong day
choices.why: Right. A stored 2 meant Tuesday and now means `Holiday`: every constant after the insert moved up by one, and the stored numbers did not.

choices.text: Nothing: each constant keeps the number of its first build
choices.why: Constants are worked out on every build, from their position; nothing remembers the old numbering.

choices.text: The build fails, because two constants now share the value 2
choices.why: No two share one: `Holiday` is 2 and `Tuesday` became 3. The compiler sees nothing wrong.

choices.text: Go renumbers the stored rows
choices.why: Go knows nothing about your database. That is why numbers that leave the program are safer written by hand.

prompt: `const primes = []int{2, 3, 5}` is refused as "not constant". A slice like that belongs in a declaration made with the keyword `___`.
hint: The other way to declare a name, which lesson 5 met first.

prompt: In one package, `main.go` imports `fmt` and `report.go` calls `fmt.Println` without importing it. What happens?
hint: Which scope does an import belong to?

choices.text: It builds, because both files are in package `main`
choices.why: That is true of `limit`, declared at package level. An import is not shared.

choices.text: It fails: `undefined: fmt`
choices.why: Right, the build fails in `report.go`. An import belongs to the one file that wrote it.

choices.text: It builds with a warning, and runs
choices.why: Go does not warn about scope; a name that is not in scope is an error.

choices.text: It builds, and panics when `report` is called
choices.why: An undefined name is found at compile time, before anything runs.

prompt: What does this print? `x := 1` then `if true { x := 2; x++ }` then `fmt.Println(x)`
hint: How many variables called `x` are there?

choices.why: That would need the `if` to change the outer `x`. Its `:=` declared a second one instead.
That treats `:=` as `=` and forgets the `++`; neither touches the outer `x` anyway.
Right. The block's `x` is a new variable that hid the outer one until the closing brace.

choices.text: Nothing: the build fails with "no new variables on left side of :="
choices.why: That error is for `:=` in the same block as the existing name. Inside the `if`, `x` is new.

prompt: Match each scope to something the lesson's programs declared there.
hint: The table at the top of section 03.

prompt: `total` stopped at `"x"` and still returned `3 <nil>`. Why `<nil>`?
hint: Count the variables called `err`.

choices.text: `strconv.Atoi` returns no error for a string it cannot read
choices.why: It did return one: the fixed version printed `strconv.Atoi: parsing "x": invalid syntax`.

choices.text: `break` resets every variable of the loop to its zero value
choices.why: `break` only leaves the loop. The error was lost because it went into a different variable.

choices.text: The loop's `:=` declared a second `err`, and the returned one was never assigned
choices.why: Right. The inner `err` held the failure and ended with the iteration; the outer one stayed `nil`.

choices.text: `return sum, err` returns whichever `err` was assigned last
choices.why: A name means the variable in scope where it is written, and at the `return` that is the outer one.

prompt: Which of these changes make `total` return the error for `"x"`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask, for each one, which `err` ends up holding the failure.

choices.text: Replace `break` with `return sum, err`
choices.why: Yes: that `err` is the inner one, the one holding the failure. It is the section's fix.

choices.text: Declare `var n int` before the loop and write `n, err = strconv.Atoi(a)`
choices.why: Yes: with `=` nothing new is declared, so the failure lands in the outer `err` that is returned.

choices.text: Rename the inner variable to `e` and keep the `break`
choices.why: The failure would then sit in `e`, and the outer `err` would still never be assigned.

choices.text: Run `go vet` before building
choices.why: `go vet` exited 0 on this program. It did not report the shadowed `err`.

prompt: A function starts with `len := 3`, and twenty lines further down it calls `len(names)`. What happens?
hint: Is `len` a keyword or a name?

choices.text: The first line is refused, because `len` is a keyword
choices.why: `len` is a predeclared name in the universe scope, so declaring a variable with it is allowed.

choices.text: It works: the parentheses make Go pick the built-in function
choices.why: The parentheses do not choose; the innermost `len` in scope is the variable.

choices.text: The call is refused: `len` is a variable of type `int` there
choices.why: Right. The variable hides the built-in until the end of the block, and an `int` cannot be called.

choices.text: It compiles and panics when the call runs
choices.why: Calling a non-function is a type error, found at compile time.

prompt: Put the five scopes in order, from the outermost to the innermost.
hint: The figure of section 03 draws them as nested boxes.

prompt: `type Config struct { Retries int; Verbose bool; Name string }` and `var cfg Config`. What does `fmt.Printf("%#v\n", cfg)` print?
hint: Each field at its own zero.

choices.text: `<nil>`
choices.why: A struct is never `nil`; only pointers, slices, maps, functions and interfaces are.

choices.text: `main.Config{Retries:0, Verbose:false, Name:nil}`
choices.why: A string's zero is `""`, not `nil`; `nil` is not a value a string can hold.

choices.text: `main.Config{Retries:0, Verbose:false, Name:""}`
choices.why: Right. Every field took its own type's zero, as `point` did in section 01.

choices.text: `main.Config{}`
choices.why: `%#v` writes every field of a struct, set or not, as the `point` lines showed.

prompt: Which of these declarations compiles?
hint: A constant is worked out before the program runs.

choices.text: `const now = time.Now()`
choices.why: A function call runs when the program does; the compiler says `time.Now()` is not constant.

choices.text: `const limit = 10 * 1024`
choices.why: Right. Arithmetic on numbers the compiler already knows gives a constant.

choices.text: `const names = []string{"ana", "bia"}`
choices.why: A slice is built at run time; this is the `primes` error again, and it belongs in a `var`.

choices.text: `n := iota`, inside `main`
choices.why: `iota` only means something inside a `const` declaration, and the compiler says so.
